opus-5.5.text:
For me, the clearest milestone is when a model genuinely discovers something new: not retrieving or recombining an answer that already exists somewhere in its training data, but working through a problem nobody has solved before and producing a result that experts can verify and build on.

We've started to see early signs of this. Models are working on hard math problems, finding bugs in large, unfamiliar codebases, and sustaining long chains of reasoning over hours rather than seconds. But the moment I'd really mark is when a model makes a contribution that a research community accepts on its own merits. That might be a new proof, a new algorithm, or a scientific insight, where the main story is the result itself and not the fact that an AI produced it.

What makes this interesting from where I sit, working on coding agents, is that software is a great proving ground. Code is verifiable. You can run it, test it, and see whether it actually works. So when an agent takes a vague, open-ended task, figures out the architecture, hits dead ends, backtracks, and lands on a solution a senior engineer would be proud of, that's a small version of novel problem solving happening every day. The jump from there to frontier research is about scaling the same capabilities: longer horizons, better judgment about what to try next, and the persistence to keep going when the first ten ideas don't work.

So I don't think it will be one dramatic moment. It'll be the point where people stop being surprised that the AI figured it out, and simply start relying on it as a collaborator on problems that matter.

r001.rationale: The response describes current and future AI capabilities, but does not say people limit expectations by extrapolating from what AI can do now.

r002.rationale: It identifies a research contribution accepted on its own merits—such as a new proof, algorithm, or scientific insight—as the milestone.

r003.rationale: It calls AI a potential collaborator, but does not state that a breakthrough achieved with human–AI collaboration qualifies when AI is indispensable.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the clearest milestone, for me, was watching a model work through a problem it had genuinely never seen before and not just produce a plausible-looking answer, but actually reason its way there over a long stretch of time. The thing I keep coming back to is the competition math and programming results, something like gold-medal performance at the International Mathematical Olympiad. Those problems are designed specifically so that you can't pattern-match your way out. They're new every year, written by people whose whole job is to make them resistant to memorization.

What mattered to me wasn't the medal itself. It was what the model had to do to get there. It had to hold a plan in its head for hours, try approaches, notice they were failing, back out, and try something else. That's qualitatively different from the earlier generation, where you'd ask a question and get one shot at an answer. Once a model can sustain effort over a long horizon and self-correct, you've crossed from "very good autocomplete" into something that looks a lot more like problem-solving.

And on the engineering side, the equivalent milestone was seeing agents like Codex take a vague task in a real codebase, one with messy constraints and no clean specification, and come back with a working change after exploring, running tests, and fixing their own mistakes. The novelty there isn't the individual steps. It's that nobody told it the steps.

So if I had to name the milestone in one line: it's when the time horizon got long enough that the model's own process started to matter more than what it had memorized. That's when I stopped thinking of these systems as answering questions and started thinking of them as doing work.

r001.rationale: The response describes current AI capabilities and milestones, but does not say people overgeneralize from those capabilities when limiting expectations of AI’s future.

r002.rationale: It cites competition results and an IMO gold-medal-level performance as evidence of problem-solving, but does not identify an AI-produced artifact valued for the breakthrough it embodies.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss human–AI collaboration or say that AI must be indispensable for a collaborative breakthrough to qualify.

astra-6.text: I think a major milestone would be an AI making a significant scientific discovery—solving a problem that people have been working on, where we don’t already know the answer. And I’d want that result to be independently verified. There’s a big difference between producing something that sounds like a new idea and producing an idea that actually works. Being able to formulate a hypothesis, test it, learn from what fails, and arrive at a discovery would be a compelling demonstration of the ability to solve novel problems.

sol-6.1.text: I think a major milestone would be an AI making a meaningful scientific discovery—solving an open problem where we don’t already know the answer. It would need to do more than generate a plausible idea: formulate a hypothesis, figure out how to test it, learn from the results, and ultimately produce something we can independently verify. That would be compelling evidence that it can help us push beyond existing knowledge.
